section_summary: This section covers the sale and rehabilitation of Japan’s cotton textile industry in 1948. Correspondence and studies discuss dollar shortages, unsold cloth, raw cotton financing, possible sales in the United States, and trade with sterling-area markets. It also includes a contract fragment, an export-bond dispute, a proposal to exchange Japanese spinning machinery for Indian materials, and the opening of a SCAP industry outlook.

subfiles.title: Proposed contract for sale of Japanese textiles
subfiles.about: Sets delivery, inspection, payment, shipping-document and buyer-representative terms for Japanese textiles.
subfiles.summary: The surviving final pages specify when title and risk pass, deadlines for ocean transport and payment, handling of bills of lading, and authority for a buyer’s representative in Japan.

subfiles.title: Consular assistance with claims on old-stock textile sales
subfiles.about: Approves requests for American consulates to help communicate and identify experts for textile-sale claims.
subfiles.summary: State has no objection to consular help with claims.

subfiles.title: Rehabilitation of Japan’s cotton textile industry
subfiles.about: Summarizes spindle capacity, cotton supply, production limits and export prospects.
subfiles.summary: Whitman estimates fewer than three million operable spindles, outlines raw-cotton needs and export expectations, and argues that textile exports could aid Japan’s recovery.

subfiles.title: Proposal for long-term agreements to sell occupied-area textiles
subfiles.about: Proposes five-year textile-purchase arrangements linked to strategic-material purchases and recovery aid.
subfiles.summary: Royall cites large unsold Japanese textile inventories and shrinking dollar markets. He asks State to approach friendly governments about agreed allocations and prices, potentially connected to strategic-material purchases and Marshall Plan assistance.

subfiles.title: Reply to Royall on occupied-area textile sales
subfiles.about: Responds to the Army’s proposal for negotiated textile sales tied to aid and strategic purchases.
subfiles.summary: State identifies dollar shortages as a central obstacle and favors arrangements allowing payment in other currencies. It declines to require aid recipients or strategic-material suppliers to reserve funds for occupied-area textiles, while offering to explore other measures with the Army.

subfiles.title: Recommendation for signature of reply to Royall
subfiles.about: Recommends signing the proposed State Department reply to Royall.
subfiles.summary: Recommends signature while summarizing why the draft rejects Royall’s proposed use of aid and stockpiling purchases.

subfiles.title: Cover letter enclosing correspondence on exportation bonds
subfiles.about: Forwards a copy of a letter to the Secretary of Agriculture about the Japanese cotton textile program.
subfiles.summary: Weaver sends Marshall a copy of his Agriculture letter.

subfiles.title: Request to reconsider retention of textile exportation bonds
subfiles.about: Asks the Commodity Credit Corporation to reconsider refusing to return buyers’ exportation bonds.
subfiles.summary: Weaver argues that retaining U.S. Commercial Company bonds treats mostly smaller buyers differently from buyers whose bonds were returned by the Japanese Board of Trade. An attached schedule compares the bonds and textile contract values.

subfiles.title: Report on the Japanese cotton textile situation
subfiles.about: Urges raw-cotton financing to keep Japanese mills operating and cautions against reliance on textile exports.
subfiles.summary: Cabot calls for prompt cotton supplies to prevent mill curtailment. He supports production within current SCAP plans but questions assumptions that cloth exports alone can secure Japan’s foreign exchange.

subfiles.title: Army views on sales of Japanese textiles in the United States
subfiles.about: Seeks State’s comments on Council of Economic Advisers views favoring commercial sales of Japanese textiles in the United States.
subfiles.summary: Draper endorses carefully priced U.S. sales and forwards Nourse’s letter and the Council staff study. He asks that the memorandum remain confidential.

subfiles.title: State reply on Japanese textile sales
subfiles.about: States general agreement with Army and Council views on Japanese textile sales.
subfiles.summary: Saltzman cites State’s earlier support for sales to any country and encloses its comments on the Jacobs mission.

subfiles.title: Routing of Draper letter and enclosures
subfiles.about: Forwards Draper’s letter for information and preparation of a reply.
subfiles.summary: Lewis asks Bowman to draft Saltzman’s reply to Draper.

subfiles.title: Council transmittal of staff study on Japanese textiles
subfiles.about: Returns documents and forwards Walter S. Salant’s staff memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Nourse forwards Salant’s study without presenting every technical judgment as an official Council finding.

subfiles.title: SCAP policy on sale of Japanese cotton textiles
subfiles.about: Examines how Japan can sell accumulated cotton textiles and obtain dollars to repay raw-cotton credit.
subfiles.summary: Salant separates the problem of finding textile markets from that of finding dollars to repay the Commodity Credit Corporation. He explores barter, changes in sourcing and aid purchases, U.S. sales and longer-term credit. He reviews the Jacobs mission’s proposals, rejecting delays, U.S.-based pricing and limits on American sales; appended tables give Japanese trade and market figures.

subfiles.title: Jacobs–Symmes–Comer report on merchandising Japanese cotton textiles
subfiles.from: Department of the Army Public Information Division; William P. Jacobs, Frederick W. Symmes and Donald Comer
subfiles.to: Public; Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Publishes the textile mission’s sixteen recommendations for financing and selling Japanese cotton textiles.
subfiles.summary: The mission describes a 300-million-yard unsold inventory and the difficulty of buying dollar cotton while selling cloth in soft-currency markets. It recommends a revolving cotton fund, wider use of Japanese sales expertise, changes to currency and pricing rules, domestic distribution of some cloth, and renewed barter. It favors established Asian and colonial markets first and proposes a limit on sales in the United States tied to dollars needed for American cotton.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about Japanese spinning-machinery sales to India
subfiles.about: Requests comment on a machinery maker’s concerns about Japan’s agreement to supply spinning spindles to India.
subfiles.summary: Martin forwards the company’s letter and asks State for comments.

subfiles.title: Interim reply to Speaker Martin
subfiles.about: Promises a substantive response after obtaining data on Japan’s textile-machinery industry.
subfiles.summary: Lovett says State is gathering data needed to answer Schaberg’s points.

subfiles.title: State response on Japan–India spinning-spindle trade
subfiles.from: Charles E. Bohlen, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the proposed Japanese spindle exports to India and answers concerns about capacity, materials and competition.
subfiles.summary: State describes the spindles as part of a broader exchange for Indian materials. It says deliveries should be feasible, appropriated U.S. materials will not be used, and the lower Japanese price reflects material costs and equipment quality. State regards textile-machinery production as part of Japan’s peaceful recovery.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Publications Analysis No. 186
subfiles.about: Encloses two copies of a SCAP Publications Analysis report dated July 10.
subfiles.summary: Forwards two copies of Publications Analysis No. 186.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of OIR Report 4710 on Far Eastern dependent markets
subfiles.about: Forwards a study of Japanese cotton textile trade with Far Eastern dependencies of European Recovery Program countries.
subfiles.summary: Suggests recovery-program offshore purchases could expand Japan’s textile trade with Malaya, the Netherlands East Indies and Hong Kong.

subfiles.title: SCAP views on the Japanese cotton industry, 1948–1949
subfiles.about: Reports SCAP forecasts for spindle rehabilitation, cotton needs, domestic allocation and export sales.
subfiles.summary: Sebald reports that reaching four million spindles before late 1949 appears unlikely and provides estimates of output and raw-cotton requirements. He describes pressure to increase domestic allotments while maintaining exports. Sterling-area negotiations may permit full sterling payment for textiles, although Japan still needs dollar receipts to pay for much of its cotton.

subfiles.title: Outlook for the Japanese Cotton Industry, 1948–1949
subfiles.about: Opens an industry outlook with recommendations on spindle rehabilitation, domestic allocation and cotton procurement.
subfiles.summary: The study recommends completing the Big Ten mills’ rehabilitation program by June 1949, raising domestic allocation to 40 percent when conditions permit, and setting 1948 cotton procurement within a stated range. The study continues beyond this section.
